transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Giles Snyder.
President Trump says he's concluded what he calls a very big trade deal with the Philippines.
It's a fair deal for both countries and we're very happy with it.
And we didn't know that that was going to take place,
but it took place very quickly and it's a magnificent deal for both.
Trump speaking at the Philippine Presidential Palace today.
He did not provide details,
but later said on social media that the deal would benefit farmers and energy businesses.
Chinese state media now reporting that Trump is now in Shenzhen, China,
where he will meet with Chinese leader Xi Jinping
and Russian president Vladimir Putin in Piers Franco-Ordonez.
This is about managing an already fragile relationship between the U.S. and China.
And I think a big topic of discussion is going to be a trade deal that is about to expire in January.
If you remember about a year ago,
that deal was part of lowering tensions amid an escalating trade war,
and it has to do with lowering tariffs and China loosening controls on rare earths.
So you can expect they're going to work on something there.
Nvidia's board says it does not intend to reinstate former CEO Jensen Huang
despite pressure from President Trump and Silicon Valley executives,
and Piers John Ruich has more.
There has been a groundswell of support for Jensen Huang,
with backers saying allegations against him have not yet been fully investigated
and he should not have had to leave the company he founded.
This week, Huang broke days of silence to say he would return to the company
if the board thought it was the right move.
But board chairman Harvey Jones poured cold water on that idea.
The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation
and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.
Interim CEO Collette Kress said Nvidia's ambitions won't change going forward.
John Ruich, NPR News.
President Trump's controversial nominee to be the Interior Department's inspector general
faces an initial Senate confirmation hearing today.
NPR's Kirk Sigler reports on the Trump loyalist who co-authored
part of the right-wing playbook Project 2025.
Trump nominated Dennis Kirk to be inspector general
at the Department of the Interior last August.
Democrats and environmentalists argue Republicans are ramming through his nomination
during the lame duck Congress.
Tim Whitehouse is with Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility.
Our concern is taxpayer and park visitor money
is flowing to politically connected donors and contractors
with no bidding, no transparency, and no answers to Congress.
Current and newly elected Democrats in the next Congress say they're eager to
investigate how contracts like those for the reflecting pool were no bid
and the Interior's secretary Doug Burgum's new strategic plan
that calls for using more federal public lands for data centers and selling some parcels.
Kirk Sigler, NPR News.
This is NPR.
Former Congresswoman Mary Peltola is the next U.S. Senator from Alaska.
According to an AP race call late last night, Peltola flipped the Senate seat
held by Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.
Her victory gives Democrats a 56 to 44 seat majority
over Republicans when the new Congress meets in January.
41-year-old Andrew Kozak pleaded not guilty in federal court yesterday
on two counts of making a threat involving explosives
and making that threat over email.
Kozak allegedly sent an email to BioUrge Renewables
saying there were bombs inside a facility in Peoria, Illinois.
The FBI says agents found an explosive device inside.
A few hours later, Ryan Denham, a member of station W-C-B-U reports.
A LinkedIn profile under Kozak's name suggests he worked at the plant as a trainee.
U.S. Attorney for Central Illinois Gregory Gilmour
says they identified Kozak as a suspect early on.
Quick action was taken. It was all hands on deck.
Agents working 24/7, including prosecutors at full court press.
Officials say the plant contains ethanol and other highly combustible chemicals.
Police ordered an evacuation of 2,500 homes and businesses
that lasted 18 hours as authorities searched inside for other bombs.
No others were found.
Making threats involving explosives is a federal felony,
carrying a potential sentence of up to 10 years.
For NPR News, I'm Ryan Denham in Peoria, Illinois.
President Trump has withdrawn his nomination of Heidi Overton
to lead the Food and Drug Administration.
That's according to a White House official
not authorized to speak publicly about the decision.
I'm Giles Snyder, and this is NPR News.

topics.text: Trump announces a big trade deal with the Philippines, without giving details
Trump heads to Shenzhen, China to meet Xi Jinping and Putin amid trade tensions
Nvidia board refuses to reinstate ousted CEO Jensen Huang despite Trump and industry pressure
Trump nominee Dennis Kirk for Interior inspector general faces initial Senate confirmation hearing
Former Rep. Mary Peltola wins Alaska Senate seat, flipping it from Republican Dan Sullivan
Andrew Kozak pleads not guilty to federal explosive threat charges over Peoria plant email
Trump withdraws nomination of Heidi Overton to lead the Food and Drug Administration
